title: A conversation in the corridor
lede: You are on placement. A resident's daughter stops you in the corridor. Choose what to say at each point and see where it goes.
intent: Learners can respond to a grieving family member in a way that keeps the conversation open, without arguing, over-promising or stepping outside their role.
goal: respond to a grieving family member in a way that keeps the conversation open, without arguing, over-promising or stepping outside your role.
setting: You are a student on placement in a residential aged care home. Frank, 84, was told this week that his cancer has spread. His daughter Leanne visits every afternoon. Today she stops you in the corridor outside his room.

nodes.say: There's been a mix-up with Dad's results. He looks better than he has in months. Can you get the doctor to redo the scan?

choices.label: "It sounds like the results came as a real shock. What did the doctor tell you?"
choices.feedback: You neither agree that there is a mistake nor argue that there is not. You name the feeling and ask what she understands, which tells you where she is.

choices.label: "I'm sorry, but the results are right. You need to accept this."
choices.feedback: Correct on the facts, but it tells her what she is allowed to feel. Denial often protects someone while the news sinks in, and pushing against it usually makes them hold on harder.

choices.label: "I'm sure it's a mistake. I'll ask them to redo it."
choices.feedback: Kind in the moment, but it is a promise you cannot keep, it steps outside your role as a student, and it strengthens a belief that will hurt more later.

nodes.say: Don't tell me what I need to do. Nobody here has told us anything straight for weeks.

choices.label: "I can hear how frustrated you are. You've been left without answers."
choices.feedback: Naming the anger lets it be said, which usually lowers it. You have not taken it personally, and you have not defended anyone.

choices.label: "That's not fair. The staff here work really hard."
choices.feedback: Defending the team is a natural reflex, but it turns her anger into an argument. Anger aimed at the person in the room is rarely about that person.

choices.label: "Let me get the nurse in charge for you."
choices.feedback: Bringing in the right person is a fair step. Done straight away, before acknowledging anything, it can feel like being handed off.

nodes.say: Later that afternoon Leanne finds you again. "The nurse said nobody is redoing the scan. Why did you tell me they would?"

choices.label: "I'm sorry. I shouldn't have said that. I wanted to help and I got it wrong."
choices.feedback: A plain apology, with no excuses, repairs more than an explanation would. It also shows her you can be trusted to tell her the truth.

choices.label: "I must have misunderstood what you were asking."
choices.feedback: It moves the mistake onto her. She will notice, and it makes the next conversation harder for whoever has it.

nodes.say: She is quieter now. "He keeps saying that if he'd stopped smoking earlier none of this would have happened. I don't know what to say to him."

choices.label: "What do you think he needs to hear from you?"
choices.feedback: It hands the question back to her, where the answer is. She knows her father. Your job is to help her find the words, not to supply them.

choices.label: "Tell him not to think like that. It's not his fault."
choices.feedback: Reassuring and well meant, but it can close the conversation he is trying to have. "If only" is how many people work through what is happening to them.

choices.label: "The doctors did say smoking was the likely cause."
choices.feedback: True, and it confirms his guilt at the moment he is most exposed to it. Accuracy is not what is needed here.

nodes.say: Leanne is quiet for a moment. "That he did alright. That he was a good dad." She thanks you and goes back into his room.
nodes.outcome: You did not fix anything, and you were not meant to. You kept the conversation open at each point, and she left with something she can do. Before your shift ends, tell your supervisor about the conversation, so the team knows where the family is.

nodes.say: Leanne nods. "Yeah. I'll tell him." She goes back into his room.
nodes.outcome: A kind conversation that stayed open. The chance you missed was to let her find her own words for her father. Tell your supervisor about the conversation before your shift ends.

nodes.say: The nurse in charge takes Leanne into the family room and closes the door.
nodes.outcome: Getting the right person involved is never wrong. Next time, try acknowledging what she is feeling first, so the handover does not feel like a brush-off.

nodes.say: Leanne turns away. "Forget it." She walks back to her father's room.
nodes.outcome: The conversation closed. That happens, even to experienced staff, and it is recoverable. Let your supervisor know what was said so someone can follow up with the family today.

teach.watchFor: Learners who look for the one magic sentence. There is not one. Every strong choice here does the same thing: it keeps the conversation open and leaves the family member in charge of their own feelings.
ask: Which poor choice was the most tempting, and why?
At which point did your role as a student matter most?

sources.label: Scenario written for this activity
sources.note: Check with a practitioner that the dialogue, the setting and the escalation advice match your placement sites' expectations.
